# Isaiah 43 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

The chapter opens with a dramatic turn from judgment (Isaiah 42:18–25) to comfort. God reassures His people of His love, protection, and future restoration from exile. It contains a courtroom challenge to the nations, a prophecy against Babylon, a promise of a "new thing," and a sharp rebuke of Israel's lukewarmness — followed immediately by astonishing mercy.

---

## v. 1 — "Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!"

- **"But now"** marks a sharp contrast from the wrath of the preceding chapter. Divine love has "won the victory" over divine wrath, and God now speaks comfort. (Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- Ellicott notes that "created thee" implies more than general creation — God created Israel to answer to "an archetype in His own purpose." To "call by name" is a mark of "individualising tenderness" and even "predestinating love." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Gill** treats this as addressed to the Christian church, the "spiritual Israel of God": the creation and formation refer to the "new creation" and regeneration in Christ. Redemption by Christ is "an antidote against the fear of any enemy." "Thou art mine" means they are His by the Father's gift, Christ's purchase, and their own voluntary self-surrender. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)**: God's ownership is personal ("called you by your name") and certain ("You are Mine"). Knowing we belong to the LORD is "a wonderful answer to fear." God would not have created, redeemed, and called us unless He intended to finish His work in us. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Spurgeon** preached that "Fear not" is a command of God that "brings its own power of performance with it." Redemption is "a well of consolation" — the redeemed have nothing whatever to fear. (Spurgeon, via CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.li.html)
- **Pulpit** notes an "ascending series of benefits": creation (out of nothing), formation (shaping what was formless), redemption (making them His own), and calling by name (conferring distinction). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)

---

## v. 2 — "When you pass through the waters… through the rivers… through the fire…"

- **Trials are inevitable**: the text says "when," not "if." Waters, rivers, and fire are metaphors for all forms of danger and affliction (Psalm 66:12). Floods overwhelm; fires consume — but God promises preservation *through* them, not necessarily *from* them. (Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Spurgeon**: "The godly have the best company in the worst places." In deep waters, God is with them; in the fire, they "shall not be burned." Where God is, all is safe. (Spurgeon via CCEL)
- **Gill**: waters and fire represent persecutions, Satan's temptations, and various afflictions. Though they come near, they "shall not overflow" — faith will not utterly fail, nor will they be separated from God's love. The promise "has been abundantly verified in the martyrs of Jesus." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Guzik** notes the image of "walking" through fire: "Walking is the pace at which you go when you are not in a hurry, when you are not concerned or alarmed." God so strengthens His people that they need not panic. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Pulpit**: A literal fulfilment is seen in the three Hebrew youths in the furnace (Daniel 3:27), but the prophecy has "a far wider scope." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Guzik** also notes Exodus imagery throughout: "I am the LORD your God" echoes Exodus 20:2, reminding readers of deliverance from Egypt.

---

## vv. 3–4 — "I give Egypt for your ransom… Because you are precious and honored in My sight… I love you"

- **Spurgeon** devoted an entire sermon ("Jehovah's Valuation of His People") to v. 3, noting God declares His own name ("the LORD thy God, the Holy One of Israel, thy Saviour") before giving His estimate of His people's worth: they are so precious He would give nations in exchange. (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jehovahs-valuation-of-his-people)
- **Ellicott**: "Speaking after the manner of men," God surrenders Egypt, Cush, and Seba to Persia (under Cambyses, c. 527–526 BC) as a "price paid" for liberating the Jews. As a man would sacrifice slaves to ransom a son, so Jehovah deals with His people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: This is a "most remarkable prophecy" — Egypt was not conquered by Persia until Cambyses, years after Cyrus's death. Human foresight could not have predicted this. "I have given" means God had already assigned these nations in His counsels as compensation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Gill**: The historical examples (Egypt at the Exodus, Ethiopia in Asa's time) are tokens that God "will sacrifice all their enemies, rather than they shall be destroyed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Guzik**: "To prove His love for His people, God was willing to give Egypt, Cush, and Seba as a ransom for Israel." This is an Old Testament parallel to John 3:16 — God's love motivates redemption. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Gill** on v. 4: The saints are precious "not that they are valuable in themselves" but because God has chosen them, betrothed them to Himself, and died for them. They are precious "in the sight of God and Christ" — compared to gold, jewels, and a pearl of great price. God's love is an "act in eternity," unchangeable. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)

---

## vv. 5–7 — "I will bring your offspring from the east… Bring My sons from afar"

- **Ellicott**: Even from Isaiah's standpoint, the dispersion was already wide — the Ten Tribes in Media, exiles under Esar-haddon, the Phoenician slave trade carrying Jews to the Greek isles. The "escort of honour" given by the nations to returning exiles is implied. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Gill** interprets this spiritually: the gathering of God's elect (both Jews and Gentiles) from all parts of the world through the preaching of the Gospel. He specifically mentions India (where Thomas preached), Europe, Ethiopia, and even "America." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: The expressions "from the east" and "from the west" must not be pressed literally. The Jewish diaspora in Isaiah's day was real but not global; Isaiah saw the fuller scattering in vision. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **John Piper (Reformed/Baptist)** on v. 7: "God created us for His glory" does not mean He needed us to become more glorious. It means He created us to *display* His glory, that it might be "known and praised." We magnify God like a telescope (making great things visible), not like a microscope (making small things look bigger). God created "out of the fullness of love," not deficiency. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-created-us-for-his-glory)
- **Guzik**: "If we have no Creator, then we are purposeless; but God has created us, and He did it for a purpose, creating us for His glory." When we glorify God, we are most fulfilled. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Pulpit**: The three verbs in v. 7 — "created," "formed," "made" — describe process from "first rough cutting to the perfecting of the work." All three acts are done for God's glory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)

---

## vv. 8–9 — "Bring out a people who have eyes but are blind…"

- **Ellicott**: The command is a "reversed echo" of Isaiah 42:18–20. Where Israel was blind and deaf by choice, now the blind and deaf (heathen, or Israel fallen into heathenism) are said to have "capacities for sight and hearing which will one day be developed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: A tribunal is imagined. Israel is summoned first as "a blind people that have eyes" (now to some extent recovered) to witness for God. Then the nations are summoned to present their case. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Gill**: Best understood as a summons to the "Heathens uncalled" — the Roman pagan empire — who were as blind and deaf as their idols, to come and plead their cause. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Guzik**: God says, "You have chosen to worship other gods. Come before Me now and justify yourself. Bring plenty of witnesses." He quotes Motyer: "imagine any litigant depending on the blind to testify to what they have seen and the deaf to what they have heard!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)

---

## vv. 10–13 — "You are My witnesses… Before Me no god was formed… I am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me"

- **Ellicott**: Israel collectively is addressed as "the servant of Jehovah." Their restoration from exile will be living proof of God's foreknowledge — He alone can say "I am He," to whom past, present, and future are one. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit** sees two distinct witnesses in v. 10: (1) faithful Israel, and (2) "My Servant whom I have chosen" — understood as the Messiah, the one true Servant of Isaiah 42:1–7, the "Faithful Witness" (Revelation 1:5). These are the two witnesses by whom God's truth is maintained. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **John Piper (Reformed)** preached an entire message on vv. 10–13, emphasizing that God nurtures our wonder at His deity ("I am God… I act and who can reverse it?") so that wonder becomes *witness*. The content of our witness is "God's exuberance for God" — His sheer existence, sovereignty, uniqueness, and saving power. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/chosen-to-know-and-believe-and-witness-that-i-am-he--2)
- **Guzik** uses v. 10 to refute Jehovah's Witnesses: "Before Me there was no God formed, nor shall there be after Me" proves there is only one true God — no "junior gods." Since Jesus is Saviour (v. 11: "besides Me there is no savior") and only Yahweh saves, Jesus must be Yahweh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Gill**: "My servant" refers to the Messiah (citing the Targum: "my servant the Messiah, in whom I am well pleased"). The prediction of future events and their accomplishment is the "evident proof of deity." On v. 13, Gill says God's purposes "cannot be disannulled; his power cannot be controlled; his work cannot be made void." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Spurgeon**: God's people are "witnesses" — they have seen and experienced what God has done. (via CCEL excerpt)

---

## vv. 14–15 — "For your sake, I will send to Babylon… even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice"

- **Ellicott**: This is the first time in "Second Isaiah" that Babylon is explicitly named. The Chaldeans' ships "used to echo with the exulting joy of sailors," but now there will be "the wailing cry of despair." Babylon, situated on the Euphrates, was "the Venice of the earlier East." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: For Israel's sake, God has already sent "Cyrus and his soldiers" in His counsels. The Chaldeans flee to their ships with cries of grief. The nautical character of Babylon is "strongly marked in the inscriptions." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Guzik**: Isaiah prophesied Babylon's judgment *before* Babylon had even conquered Judah. This demonstrates God's sovereignty over history. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Gill** (partially retrieved) treats this as prophecy of Babylon's destruction.

---

## vv. 16–17 — "who makes a way in the sea… who brings out the chariots and horses… to lie down, never to rise again"

- **Ellicott**: A "distinct echo" of Exodus 14:16 and Psalm 77:19. The return from Babylon is to be "a second Exodus from another house of bondage." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: The Exodus is recalled as a "type and pledge of the deliverance to be looked for out of Babylon." Pharaoh's host is "quenched as tow" — i.e., as a lamp wick, which a single breath extinguishes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Guzik**: Israel could be confident God was up to judging Babylon by remembering what He did at the Red Sea. The principle: "We can always justify trusting God right now by remembering the great things He has done." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)

---

## vv. 18–19 — "Do not call to mind the former things… Behold, I am about to do something new"

- **Guzik** highlights the "fascinating — and instructive — switch": vv. 16–17 told Israel to *remember* the past (the Exodus), but v. 18 says *do not remember* the former things. There is a right remembering (God's faithfulness) and a wrong remembering (being stuck in past failure, sin, and discouragement). To move forward, Israel must forsake the latter. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Pulpit**: "The old deliverance will be as nothing compared with the new." The chief glories of the second manifestation are *spiritual* — Israel returned from Babylon "will no more hanker after idols" but will have God's law in their inward parts. The "new thing" ultimately encompasses the Messianic kingdom. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Ellicott**: The literal and spiritual senses "melt into each other." God will make "a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert" — the return route through the desert will be supernaturally provided for. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Gill** interprets the "new thing" as "redemption by the Messiah, and the conversion of the Gentiles to the glory of his grace" — a work so great the Exodus should not be mentioned in comparison. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Guzik**: "Often, when God makes a promise, we worry about the details or the obstacles… God replies, 'Don't worry about it at all. I will even make a road in the wilderness.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)

---

## vv. 20–21 — "The beasts of the field will honor Me… to give drink to My chosen people. The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise"

- **Pulpit**: The animal creation participates in the benefits of restoration, and even desert beasts honor God — how much more the rest of creation. The people will "show forth God's praise" both with songs (cf. Ezra 3:9–11; Nehemiah 12:27) and by a life in accordance with His laws. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Guzik**: Declaring praise fulfills the purpose for which God created us (v. 7). The passage has in view both Israel's deliverance from Babylon *and* the ultimate deliverance brought by the Messiah (citing Poole). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)

---

## vv. 22–24 — "But you have not called on Me… you have grown weary of Me… you have burdened Me with your sins"

- **Ellicott**: The "startling abruptness" of this complaint shifts from glowing promise to dark reality. Isaiah's experience taught him there would be a dark side: "the mercies shown to the exiles would not be according to their merits, but to God's great goodness." During exile, sacrifices were suspended; the people had not compensated by true worship. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit**: The Jews in exile had largely neglected prayer. "Hard toil occupied their time. Despair made dull their hearts." They wearied of God's service. The reproach may also look back to the pre-exilic period of idolatry and neglect. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Guzik**: When we feel serving God is a "weary burden," it is "certain evidence that we are not in step with Jesus," who said His yoke is easy and burden light (Matthew 11:28–30). God's reply to those who feel "burnt out" is essentially: "You feel burdened? Try being Me! You have burdened Me with your sins." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Spurgeon** set Israel's sins "in the light of God's eternal Love." He contrasted God's sacrifice ("I gave Egypt for your ransom") with Israel's failure to sacrifice: they brought no offerings but "made Me to serve with your sins." (Spurgeon via CCEL)
- **Gill**: The sins listed are "sins of omission and commission." The people offered no true worship and instead wearied God with their iniquities. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)

---

## v. 25 — "I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more"

- **Ellicott**: The "incisive words that prove the guilt of Israel are followed by the fullest offer of pardon on repentance." God does this "for His own sake" — to manifest "the everlasting righteousness which is also the everlasting love." "Blotting out" finds an echo in Colossians 2:14. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Guzik**: Despite all their sin, God "will forgive them at the earliest opportunity. He will forget their sins." This is illustrated by the Prodigal Son (Luke 15) — the father was ready to forget all the sin as soon as the son humbly returned. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- **Spurgeon**: "Here is a great wave of mercy washing away everything that could bear witness against the people of God!" After recounting all their failures, God does not announce destruction but forgiveness. (Spurgeon via CCEL)
- **Gill**: These sins "are freely pardoned for Christ's sake." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)

---

## vv. 26–28 — "Remind Me, let us argue the matter together… Your first father sinned… So I will disgrace the princes of your sanctuary"

- **Ellicott** on v. 26: Two interpretations: (1) "Remind me, if thou canst, of thy merits; plead in thine own defence" — ironic, since they have none; or (2) "Remind me of my promise to thee, of that electing grace which called thee." The former fits the context better. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Ellicott** on v. 27: "Your first father" is best understood as Jacob (see v. 28), not Adam or Abraham. "Thy teachers" (literally "interpreters" or "mediators") refers to priests and prophets who should have been "expounders of the Divine will." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Pulpit** on v. 27: A glance back at earlier times — the ancestors sinned, and the spiritual leaders transgressed. The exile is the "well-merited punishment." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-43.html)
- **Ellicott** on v. 28: "I have profaned the princes of the sanctuary" — "holy princes" is a title for chief priests (1 Chronicles 24:5). In exile their priestly functions were "in abeyance" — they were practically desecrated. "The curse" is the *cherem* or ban (anathema), answering to Hosea 3:4. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Gill** sees vv. 26–28 as a prediction of the destruction of the Jews by the Romans: "the body and bulk of the Jewish nation were given up to destruction, because of their sins." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Based on the sources retrieved, explicit points of denominational difference on Isaiah 43 are limited, but the following can be noted:

### Reformed / Calvinistic Emphasis (Desiring God / John Piper)
- **v. 7**: The purpose of creation is God's self-exaltation — "the universe is about Me." God's glory is the "perfect harmony of all His attributes into one infinitely beautiful and personal being." God created not from deficiency but from the "fullness of love." Our joy and God's glory are not competitors: "God is glorified in us when we are satisfied in Him." (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god-created-us-for-his-glory; https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-do-i-exist)
- **vv. 10–13**: God's sovereignty is absolute: "I act and who can reverse it?" This "nurtures wonder" that becomes witness. The Reformed emphasis on God's self-glorification and absolute sovereignty is on full display. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/chosen-to-know-and-believe-and-witness-that-i-am-he--2)

### Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill)
- **Gill** consistently interprets "Jacob" and "Israel" as referring to the Christian church, the "spiritual Israel of God" — reading the OT through a strong New Testament lens. The promises of regathering are spiritualised as the ingathering of the elect through Gospel preaching, including in America. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/43.htm)
- **Spurgeon** emphasises the experiential, heartfelt dimension: "Fear not" is a command that brings "its own power of performance." He dwells on God's astonishing love for unworthy people. (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons43/sermons43.li.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- **Guzik** emphasises the practical, devotional application: the "new thing" (v. 19) as God doing fresh works that require believers to be spiritually perceptive — "Will you stay in step with My Spirit? When He leads into something new, shall you not know it?" This openness to present-tense divine activity is characteristic of Pentecostal/charismatic reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-43/)
- He also strongly defends Trinitarian orthodoxy, using vv. 10–11 to refute Jehovah's Witnesses, which is a common Pentecostal apologetic emphasis.

---

## What Was Not Found

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings**: Searches for newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org commentary on Isaiah 43 did not yield results in the searches performed. These remain unexamined.
- **Lutheran readings**: No specific Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) commentary on Isaiah 43 was retrieved.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan readings**: No specific results from wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com were found.
- **Modern scholarly readings**: bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org notes were not retrieved.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-grace readings**: No relevant results from the searched sources emerged.
